idiom_name: header/body record + explicit serializer + one binding per transport
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one message type with two sections - a header section of named, typed values (map, field table or fixed struct) and a body section of bytes or a serialized payload - and keep the two sections separately serializable so infrastructure can read the header without decoding the body. Bind the message to each transport by mapping header names onto that transport's native metadata (HTTP header fields, AMQP properties and application-properties, Kafka record headers, JMS header fields and properties) rather than by re-encoding the body; freeze the header vocabulary as a published contract and version it. Treat the body as opaque in everything except the endpoints: if a mediator needs a field, the field belongs in the header or the boundary has been drawn wrong. Where no library supplies a message type, the same structure is hand-written: a length-prefixed header frame followed by the payload, with both bounds validated on receipt.
code_sketch:
message := { headers: map<string, value>, body: bytes }

send(channel, message):
    channel.write(freeze(message.headers), message.body)   # one atomic unit

receive(channel):
    h = parse_headers(channel.read_header_frame())          # infrastructure-readable
    b = channel.read_body(h.body_length)                    # opaque payload
    return { headers: h, body: b }
pitfalls: Skipping the body-length/bound information in the header turns the body boundary into guesswork; every receiver must be able to split header from body without parsing the payload.
Letting mediators mutate header values they do not own (routing keys, correlation ids) silently changes semantics for later hops.
Freezing neither the header vocabulary nor the body content type makes the 'portable' message unreadable for the next team that implements the same boundary.

Wrong move: Trusting inbound routing or identity headers as authenticated claims -> an untrusted producer can steer delivery or impersonate a tenant -> instead authenticate or sign at the channel and validate an allowlist of control headers before routing.

Wrong move: Copying every external header into framework control metadata -> header injection can redirect routes, invoke unintended behavior or leak data -> instead filter inbound names and map only an explicit allowlist into internal headers.

Wrong move: Putting large or business payloads in headers -> broker limits, repeated serialization and split ownership make delivery brittle -> instead keep headers bounded to technical metadata and put domain data in the typed body (or use Claim Check for bulk).
